title: Hosted API — TCP ephemeral port exhaustion postmortem
content:
Summary:
On 2026-06-10 between ~09:12–11:05 UTC we observed a global P0 outage for the Hosted API that manifested as elevated request latency, amplified 5xx rates, and failed streaming connections. Impact hit both the REST generation endpoint and streaming websocket/proxy paths. User-facing symptoms included high tail latency for non-streaming requests and a 30–60% failure rate for streaming sessions.

Immediate impact: ~18% of requests returned 5xx, streaming session setup failed at ~45% rate, and average p95 latency increased from 85ms to 1.2s across affected regions. Estimated customer impact window: 09:12–10:47 UTC (majority), with recovery actions continuing until 11:05 UTC.

What happened (brief):
We misdiagnosed an upstream application regression initially; root cause was TCP ephemeral port exhaustion on a subset of ingress nodes causing socket allocation failures and connection teardown behavior (lots of TIME_WAIT + ephemeral port reuse delays). This led to client connection setup failures and high error rates from our edge proxies (Envoy/haproxy) and streaming muxers.

Timeline (UTC):
- 09:08 — Pager triggers: elevated 5xx and p95 latency on hosted-api production metrics.
- 09:12 — First on-call ack; initial triage shows spike in tcp connection errors on edge nodes.
- 09:20 — Traffic shift experiments (manual small-scale reroute) show fewer errors when excluding a subset of nodes.
- 09:32 — Deep-dive into node-level netstat shows extremely high counts of sockets in TIME_WAIT and many ephemeral ports consumed on nodes in us-west-2.
- 09:40 — Mitigation: removed affected nodes from LB rotation (drain) and scaled up replacement nodes. Immediate 5xx rate dropped from 18% to 6%.
- 10:05 — Root cause identified as ephemeral port exhaustion due to a recent Envoy config change that reduced connection reuse (connection_idle_timeout bumped down) combined with a backend client library which created short-lived outbound connections per request.
- 10:25 — Temporary OS-level tuning applied on edge: expanded ip_local_port_range and reduced TIME_WAIT duration via tcp_tw_reuse/tcp_fin_timeout where safe.
- 10:47 — Majority of traffic routes stable; ongoing monitoring.
- 11:05 — Post-incident clean up and follow-ups assigned.

Detection and monitoring notes:
- Alerts that fired: hosted-api-5xx-rate-p95, hosted-api-p95-latency, edge-tcp-socket-errors. The edge-tcp-socket-errors alert had a high threshold and only tripped late.
- Missing: no dedicated metric for ephemeral port exhaustion (eg. ephemeral ports available per node) and no alert on sustained high TIME_WAIT counts.
- Logs: Envoy reported ECONNRESET/EMFILE during peaks on affected nodes; kernel logs showed allocation failures indicating ephemeral port range saturation.

Root cause analysis:
Primary cause:
1) Envoy upstream connection reuse was inadvertently reduced in a config change rolled out two days prior (PR #1419). The change decreased the connection idle window and introduced more frequent upstream connection churn.
2) At the same time, a backend client library (used by a routing plugin) created new outbound connections per request rather than reusing pooled connections for short-lived internal RPCs. This combination amplified ephemeral port consumption on ingress nodes.
3) Our default ephemeral port range on nodes (32768-60999) became exhausted under the multiplied connection churn pattern. TIME_WAIT accumulation prevented immediate reuse.

Contributing factors:
- Lack of a canary that measured node-level socket/resource metrics when rolling the Envoy config. The config roll was tested on traffic but did not capture peak connection churn patterns.
- No alert on high TIME_WAIT or low ephemeral port availability.
- Edge autoscaling behavior replaced nodes slowly; draining plus graceful termination left TIME_WAIT sockets lingering longer.
- kube-proxy/node NAT behavior: many outbound connections from different pods shared node ephemeral ports; high fanout worsened exhaustion.

Immediate mitigations performed during incident:
- Drained and removed the most affected nodes from the LB pool to reduce error surface.
- Scoped rollback of recent Envoy config change to previous stable connection idle timing across ingress fleet. (Rollback PR link in linked_artifacts.)
- Applied temporary kernel tunables on affected nodes: expanded ip_local_port_range to 20000-65535 and reduced tcp_fin_timeout to 30s where safe. Enabled tcp_tw_reuse on non-isolated hosts.
- Scaled up ingress capacity while rebalancing traffic away from high-TIME_WAIT nodes.

Permanent remediation plan (short-term, 0–2 weeks):
1) Revert and rework the Envoy config change to preserve connection reuse semantics and add explicit connection pooling tests to CI. Owner: Marco Ruiz. Target: 2026-06-17.
2) Update backend client libraries to use connection pooling or keepalive by default. Create a migration checklist for services using the routing plugin. Owner: Aisha Patel. Target: 2026-06-24.
3) Add per-node ephemeral port utilization metric and TIME_WAIT gauge; create alert when ephemeral ports free < 10% for >5m. Owner: Li Wei (observability). Target: 2026-06-15.
4) Implement a pre-deploy canary job that exercises connection churn at scale (synthetic load test) before rolling changes to Envoy/edge. Owner: Eng-Release. Target: 2026-06-21.
5) Harden autoscaler and drain behavior: ensure node replacement is faster and that we proactively rebalance existing sockets across healthy nodes. Owner: SRE-runbook. Target: 2026-06-30.

Longer-term mitigations (2–12 weeks):
- Evaluate using SO_REUSEPORT and connection multiplexing upgrades to limit ephemeral port usage.
- Explore redesign of certain internal RPC paths to use long-lived multiplexed connections (gRPC channels with keepalive).
- Capacity planning: adjust baseline ephemeral port range and consider per-pod SNAT mapping changes to reduce NAT collisions.

Runbook changes (explicit):
- Add a new runbook section: "Ephemeral port exhaustion and TIME_WAIT surge" with step-by-step diagnostics (netstat, ss, /proc/net/ip_local_port_range, conntrack status), immediate mitigations, and safe OS tunables. Owner: Connor Blake. Target: 2026-06-14.
- Update the incident checklist to include: check kernel allocation errors (EMFILE, ENOBUFS), per-node TIME_WAIT, and env metrics for Envoy upstream connection churn.
- Add clear guidance on when it's safe to alter ip_local_port_range vs. when to address connection reuse at application/proxy layer.

Alerts and dashboards to add (names & thresholds):
- node/ephemeral-ports/available (alert when < 10% for 5m)
- node/time-wait/count (alert when > 50k sockets for 10m)
- envoy/upstream/connection-reuse-rate (detect sudden drops)
- hosted-api/edge/accept-failures (lower threshold to catch earlier)

Communication timeline (stakeholders and messaging):
- 09:30 — Initial incident channel (#sre-incident) with public-facing incident banner drafted (owner: oncall).
- 10:00 — Customer-facing status page update: noted increased errors and active mitigation.
- 11:15 — Internal postmortem draft shared with eng-sre and platform-eng for review.

Metrics & follow-up verification plan:
- After changes, run a 48-hour smoke window with synthetic connection churn tests to validate ephemeral port headroom.
- Monitor the new ephemeral port metric for 7 days and require no alert fires for a rolling 72-hour window before closing the ticket.

Owners & action items (short form):
- Marco Ruiz — Rework Envoy config and CI connection tests. (JIRA-4567)
- Aisha Patel — Client library pooling audit + fixes.
- Li Wei — Dashboards/alerts for ephemeral port and TIME_WAIT.
- Connor Blake — Update/runbook and playbook steps.
- Grace Lin (owner) — Coordinate postmortem, verify mitigations, close incident.

Lessons learned (concise):
- Connection-level regressions may not be visible in request-level metrics until resource exhaustion becomes severe; we need node-level networking telemetry in our standard SLO dashboards.
- Small timing/config changes to proxies can have outsized impact when combined with inefficient client behavior. Canary tests must emulate worst-case churn.
- Having a fast, safe rollback path for edge config is critical; we rolled back quickly and that substantially reduced impact.

Appendix (commands & quick checks used during triage):
- ss -s
- ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l  # count TIME_WAIT
- cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range
- sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="20000 65535"
- sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout=30
- journalctl -u envoy | grep EMFILE

Notes to future on-callers:
- If you see streaming setup errors + high TIME_WAIT, prioritize checking ephemeral port ranges before assuming application bug. Draining nodes is an effective short-term surgical mitigation.

Status: final.
